claims.text: Conventional metallic rollers and guide plates rapidly corrode and erode during prolonged direct exposure to high-temperature molten aluminum.
A high-purity, high-alumina refractory ceramic coating can be deposited on equipment components by thermal spraying or chemical vapor deposition.
Hot-dip aluminum plating components typically encounter molten aluminum at temperatures above approximately 600–700 °C.
The equipment components remain in continuous and prolonged contact with molten aluminum.
An engineered alumina-based coating physically and chemically separates the metallic substrate from molten aluminum.
Dense surface films can improve resistance to high-temperature degradation.
High-alumina ceramics have a sufficiently high melting point to remain stable during exposure to molten aluminum.
High-alumina ceramics are chemically inert toward molten aluminum.
The alumina-based coating limits reaction between molten aluminum and the underlying metallic substrate.
The alumina-based coating limits penetration of molten aluminum.
The coating prevents interdiffusion and erosion at the molten-aluminum/substrate interface.
Preventing interfacial reaction, penetration, and erosion preserves the structural integrity of the equipment.
High-alumina-coated components will have significantly lower surface-degradation rates than uncoated components under identical conditions.
High-alumina-coated components will have longer service lives than uncoated components.
Coating adhesion strength and thermal-shock resistance may limit performance in operating conditions.
Repeated thermal cycling may produce microcracks in the coating.
